source_text: Yeah, so unblocks *might* be witten down somewhere in some of the missions or excursions, but I haven't put a great deal of effort into clarifying those semantics, so the fact that we have trouble recovering them may be just because they aren't actually there.  But we can infer, e.g., from the fact that I'm working on E-aif-cascade right now that I must think it has high priority and must think it unblocks something.  Similarly, M-diagramprover is connected to a bunch of other things; it's not a "blocker" but an enabler of those things (i.e. it doesn't need to be 'finished' to be useful, and often I work on 2 things at once, e.g., upgrading diagramprover to accomodate Lean work as well as cascade work).   If we wanted to make a really rigorous study of which missions depend on which and in which ways, that would be a big project.  But to make a first cut shouldn't be too hard; indeed, that again shows that the outer-loop-cascade can be improved over time, so minimising G is also "subject to constraints" i.e. a deep-dive to fully plan all of the work across all time is actually not a good use of time and energy.

reply_text:
㊥ (gist) Taken as guidance rather than as a defect in the data: if `unblocks` was never written down, B1b will mostly confirm that, and the first cut comes from behaviour. I added B1c to the excursion (futon2 `55c39bb0c`) — revealed attention and co-work, from records that already exist — and recorded your enabler/blocker distinction and the "subject to constraints" point as the frame for B3. codex-33 is still on B1b (its report and script are sitting untracked in the tree, not yet committed); B1c follows it.

㊢ ("we can infer … from the fact that I'm working on E-aif-cascade right now") The records for that inference are already in Cascade Live, just not read as such: `:lineage` is 126 dispatch records `{agent target session at dispatched-by}` — the very field B1 had to set aside because it is not predecessor/successor — and its top targets today are `diagramprover` 25, `apm-demonstration` 22, `the-perfect-crime` 14, `convert-operator-turns-to-patterns` 7, `象-2000` 6; the first lineage row is this excursion, dispatched by me to codex-33 an hour ago. The operator side is the turn store's "mission the operator was working under" (the `turn-traced` view). B1c reads both per item, keeps them apart, and reports ρ against the occurrence count and against B1's coupling measure.

🈖 ("not a 'blocker' but an enabler") That is a different relation again, and B1c names it so: *co-work* — items targeted by one session, by one agent within a day, or named together in one operator turn — is undirected and says "these are worked together", which is your diagramprover-with-Lean-and-cascades case; `unblocks` is directed and says "this must advance for that to"; coupling through shared patterns (B1) is a third. The proposal in B1c is that attention becomes the `unblocks` token's first-cut value as an *enabler weight*, superseded by a declaration wherever one exists, and never called a dependency.

㊣ ("a deep-dive to fully plan all of the work across all time is actually not a good use of time") Agreed, and it is already the shape of the machinery: G is scored to a horizon (R13), the field is whatever HEAD holds, and §5a has the outer cascade refined as runs return rather than specified in advance. B3 will be written as the first cut — the squares as they can be filled today, typed absences where they cannot — not as the rigorous dependency study.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: (gist) Recorded (futon2 `d8c85edf8`): shares-patterns and unblocks are two tokens with different semantics — `@how` generalised and `@why` generalised — and the Cascade Live–based simplified cascade is the outer driver. B1's number is the `@how` one; the centrality you mean is the `@why` one, and no source holds it at HEAD, so I added B1b to find what could.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: ("those have different semantics") Yes, and the two directions already carry the distinction in claude-17's §7: `@why` is the pattern's own author saying what the pattern answers, read *upward* to say why an unmet pattern matters; `@how` is an editor naming the methods, read *downward*. For items: "X unblocks Y" means Y's `@why` points at X — Y goes from unanswered to answered when X completes — and "X shares patterns with Y" is that both reach for the same methods. The first is dependency; the second is coupling. B1 measured coupling (ρ 0.896 with the live occurrence count, so the click's current "centrality" is coupling too).

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-2
previous_reply_acts.text: (B1b, next discovery after B2's amendment returns) Three candidate sources for an inter-item `@why`, kept apart: (i) cross-references in the 107 documents to other M-/E-/T- ids, each classified by the cue around it (`depends on`, `blocked by`, `feeds`, `prerequisite`, `see`) and cited by line; (ii) any lifecycle field that names a predecessor or consumer; (iii) the library's 545 `why` edges lifted to items through applied patterns, reported as a *derived* relation only. Plus a one-paragraph proposal for how an item would *declare* what rests on it (`cascades/declared-skeleton`: declare only what you would defend in review) — a derived relation being at best a prompt for a declaration. B3 then pastes in an `unblocks-reading` square that emits a typed absence until the relation exists, and a separate `shares-patterns` square whose token is consumed only if you want coupling scored at all.
